stories.title: The great grain pivot: Japan’s changing relationship with rice
stories.summary: Japan's rice consumption has dropped significantly since 1962 due to changing diets, demographic shifts, and rising prices caused by environmental challenges and increased foreign demand. Yamagata, a key rice-producing region, combines traditional farming with advanced technology like drones and robots to address labour shortages and climate change. Innovations include heat-tolerant rice strains, new rice-based products, and circular farming methods, aiming to sustain rice's cultural importance and economic value amidst evolving consumption patterns. Growing up in Singapore, I was told that every grain of rice left uneaten on my plate would leave a pockmark on my face. In Japan, children are taught to honour their bowls through a folk belief that “seven gods” reside in every grain. Leftovers show disrespect for the natural elements and human labour that went into the crop. Rice has long been the cultural spine and soul of many Asian societies.

stories.title: Clean-up of illegal waste supersite costs taxpayers £6m
stories.summary: The clear-up of one of England's largest illegal waste tips has been completed - landing taxpayers with a £6m bill. The government has vowed to recoup the clearance costs for the Kidlington dump in Oxfordshire - and seven other sites - from the criminals responsible. In 2025, around 22,000 tonnes of domestic and commercial rubbish was dumped at the spot, between the River Cherwell and the A34. It is one of nearly 30 so-called "supersites" first uncovered by a BBC investigation. The government, which launched a crackdown on waste crime last week, said it would do more to force criminals to pay for clean-up operations by confiscating their money and assets. But figures obtained by the BBC show that, in the past five years, the Environment Agency has so far managed to claw back just over £7m from waste criminals using Proceeds of Crime Act (Poca) confiscation orders. Campaigners have labelled the amount taken from convicted criminals as "derisory" while the Country Land and Business Association (CLA), which represents rural landowners, asked: "Where is the deterrent?" The amount paid by criminals so far was revealed by an Environmental Information Regulations (EIR) request to the Environment Agency by the BBC. It shows there have been 66 confiscation orders between January 2021 and March 2026, totalling £7.3m. Fourteen orders have yet to be fully paid, leaving around £1.4m still to be recovered. The figures cover those larger illegal sites for which the Environment Agency is responsible, and do not include confiscation orders for smaller fly-tipping offences, which fall under the remit of local authorities. Baroness Sheehan, who chairs the House of Lords environment and climate change committee, said the figures obtained by the BBC showed "consistent, decisive enforcement" was lacking.

stories.title: Australian police arrest two men accused of widespread open-source software hacking
stories.summary: Aug 27 - Australian police announced charges on Thursday against two men accused of participating in a cybercrime syndicate that targeted widely used open-source software to compromise thousands of global businesses. The Australian men face a combined 14 charges for their alleged roles in TeamPCP, a hacking collective that inserted malicious code into popular tools to compromise businesses, according to a statement from the Australian Federal. Police. Some of the businesses were later extorted, according to a July FBI advisory. The police did not name the men, but the Australian Broadcasting Corporation identified them as Ruben Ian Thomson, 21, and Louis Michael Gaebler, 23. Nick Scerri, a lawyer for Thomson, did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside of normal business hours. Reuters could not immediately find an attorney for Gaebler. The malicious code potentially compromised more than 1,000 organizations globally, enabling the theft of more than 500,000 credentials and more than 300 gigabytes of data, according to police. The police said they conducted a parallel investigation into the men with the FBI starting in April after receiving information from multiple unnamed cybersecurity threat assessment companies. “We are proud to work with the Australian Federal Police and the Western Australia Police Force to impose cost on criminal actors and combat the growing threat of software supply-chain attacks,” FBI Cyber Division Assistant Director Brett Leatherman said in the police statement. The FBI declined further comment.

stories.title: Savings banks' H1 net nearly triples; delinquency rate advances
stories.summary: SEOUL, Aug. 28 (Yonhap) -- Savings banks' first-half net profit nearly tripled f...
article_sentences: Savings banks' first-half net profit nearly tripled from a year earlier, aided by a decline in loan-loss reserves and investment returns, data showed Friday.

Their combined net profit nationwide reached 766 billion won (US$553 million) in the January-June period, sharply up from a net profit of 257 billion won a year earlier, according to their trade association.
Their asset soundness deteriorated, with the delinquency rate coming in at 6.26 percent at the end of June, up from 6.04 percent at the end of December.
The rate on corporate loans rose 0.38 percentage point from six months earlier to 8.38 percent, while that on household loans fell 0.07 percentage point to 4.6 percent over the cited period.
Their average capital adequacy ratio stood at 15.73 percent at the end of June, down 0.12 percentage point from six months earlier, the data showed.
Their total assets stood at 126 trillion won at the end of June, up 2.6 trillion won from end-December.
